content: 1. Rapid immune reconstitution following antiretroviral therapy (ART) has been documented in individuals with AIDS, as reported in a 2011 study published in AIDS (Volume 25, Pages 345–355). 2. Early initiation of antiretroviral therapy in infants has been shown to significantly improve neurodevelopmental outcomes, according to a 2012 study by Laughton et al., published in AIDS (Volume 26, Pages 1685–1690). 3. A 2013 study by Williams et al., published in AIDS (Volume 27, Pages 1959–1970), examined the timing of pubertal onset in children with perinatal HIV infection during the era of combination antiretroviral therapy. 4. Szubert et al. (2015) investigated pubertal development in HIV-infected African children receiving first-line antiretroviral therapy, with findings published in AIDS (Volume 29, Pages 609–618). 5. Picat et al. (2013) developed a cohort-based model to predict long-term CD4 reconstitution patterns in HIV-infected children starting antiretroviral therapy in sub-Saharan Africa. This study was published in PLOS Medicine (Volume 10, Article e1001542). 6. Lewis et al. (2012) explored the effects of age and CD4 count at the initiation of antiretroviral therapy on long-term T-cell reconstitution in HIV-infected children, as reported in The Journal of Infectious Diseases (Volume 205, Pages 548–556). 7. A 2014 study by Desmonde et al., published in AIDS (Volume 28, Pages 1645–1655), highlighted the association between the age at antiretroviral therapy initiation and the 24-month immune response in West African HIV-infected children. 8. Patel et al. (2008) examined the long-term effects of highly active antiretroviral therapy on CD4+ cell evolution in children and adolescents with HIV, with findings published in Clinical Infectious Diseases (Volume 46, Pages 1751–1760). 9. Kenny et al. (2015) presented evidence that structural cardiovascular changes in HIV-infected children in Zambia and Uganda are reversible. These findings were shared at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in Seattle, WA. 10. Wintergerst et al. (2008) evaluated the antiviral efficacy, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics of efavirenz in an unselected cohort of HIV-infected children, as reported in The Journal of Antimicrobial Chemotherapy (Volume 61, Pages 1336–1339). 11. Nachega et al. (2007) demonstrated that adherence to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor-based HIV therapy is strongly associated with virologic outcomes, as published in Annals of Internal Medicine (Volume 146, Pages 564–573). 12. The PLATO II project team (2011) conducted a retrospective cohort study on the risk of triple-class virological failure in children with HIV, with results published in The Lancet (Volume 377, Pages 1580–1587). 13. Penazzato et al. (2013) provided healthcare worker perspectives on pediatric antiretroviral treatment, contributing to the WHO 2013 consolidated guidelines. This information is accessible online. 14. Koller et al. (2015) examined immunodeficiency in children starting antiretroviral therapy across low-, middle-, and high-income countries, as reported in The Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (Volume 68, Pages 62–72). 15. A study on the cost of universal access to pediatric and adolescent antiretroviral treatment in Zambia (2014–2018) was published online in 2015. 16. Barker and Mate (2012) emphasized the need for significant improvements in maternal and child health services to eliminate mother-to-child HIV transmission, as reported in Health Affairs (Volume 31, Pages 1489–1497). 17. The ARROW trial team (2013) compared routine versus clinically driven laboratory monitoring and first-line antiretroviral therapy strategies in African children with HIV. The findings were published in The Lancet (Volume 381, Pages 1391–1403). 18. Baeten et al. (2015) reported near elimination of HIV transmission in a demonstration project combining PrEP and ART, presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in Seattle, WA. 19. Grant et al. 20. Martin et al. 21. Baeten et al. (2012) demonstrated the efficacy of antiretroviral prophylaxis for HIV prevention in heterosexual men and women, as published in The New England Journal of Medicine (Volume 367, Pages 399–410). 22. Choopanya et al. (2013) conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial on antiretroviral prophylaxis for HIV prevention among injecting drug users in Bangkok, Thailand, with findings published in The Lancet (Volume 381, Pages 2083–2090). 23. Grant et al. 24. Marrazzo et al. 25. Peterson et al. (2007) conducted a phase 2, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial on tenofovir disoproxil fumarate for HIV prevention in women, as published in PLOS Clinical Trials (Volume 2, Article e27). 26. Thigpen et al. 27. Van Damme et al. 28. 29. Grohskopf et al. (2013) conducted a randomized trial on the clinical safety of daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate among HIV-uninfected men who have sex with men in the United States, as published in The Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes (Volume 64, Pages 79–86). 30. 31. Consolidated guidelines on HIV prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations were published by the WHO in 2015. 32. Marrazzo et al. (2014) provided recommendations for HIV prevention in clinical care settings, as published in JAMA (Volume 312, Pages 390–409). 33. Fonner et al. 34. Hoagland et al. (2015) reported on PrEP uptake and associated factors among men who have sex with men and transgender women in the PrEP Brasil demonstration project, presented at the IAS conference in Vancouver, Canada. 35. Martin et al. (2014) examined renal function in participants of the Bangkok Tenofovir Study, with findings published in Clinical Infectious Diseases (Volume 59, Pages 716–724). 36. Solomon et al. 37. Liu et al. 38. Van de Vijver et al. 39. Marcus et al. 40. Guest et al. (2008) examined changes in sexual risk behavior among participants in a PrEP HIV prevention trial, as reported in Sexually Transmitted Diseases (Volume 35, Pages 1002–1008). 41. Gomez et al. 42. Hoagland et al. (2015) presented findings on PrEP uptake among men who have sex with men and transgender women in the PrEP Brasil demonstration project at the IAS conference in Vancouver, Canada. 43. Médecins Sans Frontières published the 17th edition of Untangling the Web of Antiretroviral Price Reductions in 2014. 44. Bekker et al. (2015) compared daily and non-daily PrEP dosing in African women as part of the HPTN 067/ADAPT Cape Town study, presented at the Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections in Seattle, WA. 45. Henderson et al. (2015) analyzed oral PrEP adherence in the TDF2 open-label extension in Botswana, presented at the IAS conference in Vancouver, Canada. 46. Mannheimer et al. (2015) compared daily and intermittent PrEP dosing for HIV prevention in men who have sex with men and transgender women in New York City as part of the HPTN 067/ADAPT study, presented at the IAS conference in Vancouver, Canada. 47. Holtz et al. (2015) compared daily and non-daily PrEP dosing in Thai men who have sex with men in Bangkok, Thailand, as part of the HPTN 067/ADAPT study, presented at the IAS conference in Vancouver, Canada. 48. Liu et al. (2015) reported on adherence, sexual behavior, and HIV/STI incidence among men who have sex with men and transgender women in the U.S. PrEP Demonstration Project, presented at the IAS conference in Vancouver, Canada. 49. Hosek et al. (2015) conducted a PrEP demonstration project and safety study for young men who have sex with men in the United States (ATN 110), presented at the IAS conference in Vancouver, Canada. 50. Machtinger et al. (2015) highlighted the promise of trauma-informed primary care in transitioning from treatment to healing, as published in Women's Health Issues (Volume 25, Pages 193–197). 51. Cottrell et al. (2014) developed a novel pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model to predict effective Truvada® PrEP dosing strategies, presented at the R4P conference in Cape Town, South Africa. 52. Ford et al. 53. Ehrhardt et al. (2015) reviewed evidence on breastfeeding while taking lamivudine or tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, as published in Clinical Infectious Diseases (Volume 60, Pages 275–279). 54. WHO provided technical briefs on the surveillance of antiretroviral drug toxicity within treatment programs, accessible online in 2015. 55. Consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services were published by the WHO in 2015. 56. 57. The Clinical Guideline Development Group (2015) declared no conflicts of interest during the development of WHO guidelines on ART and PrEP.
